item.title: Aulico: Learn to Invest with AI
Show HN: Crulon – Business phone where AI does the work, humans make the calls
item.description:
Hi HN, I’m Rayhan. Crulon is a business phone system where an AI agent answers the line and your team works alongside it. You can talk with our demo agent right in your browser, no sign-up: https://crulon.ai/#talk

Why I built it: I’ve spent eight years as a software and network engineer, mostly building tools for internet providers, and kept watching small support teams lose customers in the seams. Calls missed after hours. Calls passed from a bot to a person who had to start over. Most voice AI products are a bot sitting on someone else’s phone line, so a handoff means forwarding to another number and losing the context. We built the phone system and the agent as one thing.

What that gets you:

The handoff happens inside the same system. When something isn’t the AI’s job, it asks the caller, then rings your team (in the browser or on a desk phone) with a note on why they’re calling. Live calls: anyone with permission can listen to an AI call (no one on the call can hear them) and take it over. It’s the same call, with no transfer and no hold music; the AI just leaves. Tools: the agent can call any API you define in an Action builder (look up the caller, open a ticket), and it checks with the caller before changing anything. Outbound campaigns: the agent works through a call list for reminders, renewals and follow-ups, and puts interested people through to your team. SIP desk phones, and bring-your-own-carrier so you can keep your numbers. If you run out of AI minutes, calls follow your fallback route (ring the team, voicemail) instead of dropping, and the refused call isn’t billed.

How it’s built, briefly: calls come in over SIP into Call Flows (menus, queues, schedules), and your team answers in the browser or on SIP desk phones. Each agent runs on one of two engines. Classic transcribes, thinks, then speaks, so you get exact wording and English, Spanish and French. Live is a full-duplex speech model that listens while it talks and hands tool work to a second model. One fun problem with that split was teaching the agent when to hang up, which I wrote up here: https://crulon.ai/blog/teaching-a-voice-agent-to-hang-up

It isn’t a CRM; it works alongside yours. Built-in Apps connect it to systems like billing and network tools, and anything with a web API plugs in through the Action builder.

Pricing is per seat ($24, $49 or $89 a month) with a pool of AI minutes; human calls are included. If you sign up this month, HN30 takes 30% off the first 3 months.

I’ll be here all day. Try the agent, try to trip it up, and tell me what you’d want from a phone system like this.

item.title: Show HN: Weir - Catch credential leaks in the AI agents you build and use
item.description:
Hi HN. Weir is for one problem: credentials crossing the boundaries of your AI agent.

For agents you build, Weir plants fake credentials where real ones would live, runs the agent's normal flows, and checks what comes out: telemetry, logs, console output, model requests, and requests to other services. It looks for those exact values, including common encoded forms, and reports where they went without printing the credential.

pip install weir-scan weir canary judge --sample

That sample shows a planted key leaking into a trace. On your own agent: pip install weir-run.

For agents you use, Weir can inventory your real credentials (it stores keyed fingerprints, never the values) and show when one enters your session or leaves in a tool call. Right now, this is supported for Claude Code. Its optional hook redacts those known credentials from tool results before the model sees them. Setup is weir statusline setup, on Linux and macOS for now.

So the two modes are deliberately different:

Build: plant → run → prove where the credential went. Use: observe → warn → optionally redact before the model sees it.

The test mode is deterministic and offline. On Linux it can also run the agent without outside network access, so direct exfiltration attempts are caught. If a required path wasn't exercised, Weir reports incomplete, never clean.

It doesn't try to detect every possible secret. It matches known whole values, so hashed, split, truncated, or otherwise transformed credentials aren't covered. The Claude Code hook only protects the tool-result boundary: it can't undo a credential already pasted into the conversation, and a failed command's output reaches the model as is.

Apache-2.0, no model in the loop, and Weir itself sends nothing anywhere. It found GHSA-j7qq-vr8c-xvw3 in MLflow (fixed in 3.17.0).

Built with AI assistance; every security finding was reproduced before I reported it.
